This vignette describes how njord builds a modelled UK windstorm loss from
public data, designs parametric covers on it and measures their basis risk.
Its results are computed from the small files in `inst/extdata/`, so it
builds from a fresh checkout without the raw data or a CDS account.

```{r setup}
library(njord)
```

## Data

### ERA5 windstorm reanalysis

Hazard data come from the Copernicus Climate Change Service (C3S) Enhanced
Windstorm Service (EWS) dataset
(`sis-european-wind-storm-reanalysis`; Copernicus Climate Change Service,
2025), derived from the ERA5 global
reanalysis (Hersbach et al., 2020).

For each identified storm event the dataset provides:

- **Footprints** — the maximum 10-metre wind gust (m s⁻¹) over a
  72-hour window centred on the storm's peak land impact,
  on a 0.25° × 0.25° grid (~28 km). Njord uses the native ERA5
  resolution (0.25°) product. Each footprint is restricted to a
  1000 km radius around the storm track to avoid
  cross-contamination between contemporaneous events.

- **Track catalogue** — 6-hourly positions, mean sea level pressure and
  10 m gust speed at the storm centre for all tracked systems 1940–2025.
  Two tracking algorithms are available: *Hodges* (TRACK; Hodges, 1995, 1999)
  which follows 850 hPa relative vorticity and *TempestExtremes*
  which tracks MSLP minima. Njord uses the Hodges product, consistent with
  CLIMADA's default configuration and Mishra et al. (2026).

- **Summary indicators** — pre-computed annual storm counts, mean gust,
  Storm Severity Index (SSI), normalised SSI, area ratio and wind gust
  ratio, aggregated by NUTS region (NUTS0/1/2) and wind speed threshold
  (0, 15.6, 20, 25 m s⁻¹) for 1940–2025 (~170 000 rows).

The footprint archive (downloaded via the `ecmwfr` package) currently
comprises **721 monthly zip files** (from footprints_hodges_194002.zip through to
footprints_hodges_202604.zip) each containing one or more NetCDF footprint
files for storms active in that calendar month.

## Vulnerability model

The **Schwierz et al. (2010)** damage model is used to estimate the mean
damage ratio (MDR) as a function of wind gust speed $v$:

$$\text{MDR}(v) = \text{MDD}(v) \times \text{PAA}(v)$$

where MDD (mean damage degree) is the expected fraction of asset value
destroyed given that the asset is affected and PAA (percentage of assets
affected) is the probability that an asset at this location suffers any
damage at all. Both are empirically derived nonlinear lookup tables,
originally calibrated against UK insurance losses from named storms in the
period 1987–1990 (Schwierz et al., 2010) and subsequently validated across
multiple European countries.

The model is implemented in the open-source
[CLIMADA](https://climada-python.readthedocs.io/) platform (ETH Zurich;
Aznar-Siguan and Bresch, 2019) as `ImpfStormEurope.from_schwierz()`; njord
uses the same curve nodes (`schwierz_mdr()`).

The MDR surface is multiplied pointwise with the LitPop asset exposure
(Eberenz et al., 2020) — a globally consistent dataset that disaggregates
national asset values in proportion to nightlight intensity × population,
used here at 150 arcsec (~5 km) and summed to the 0.25° footprint grid —
to yield modelled monetary losses per grid cell and per event.
The sum over a region is the storm's **modelled loss** there, the benchmark
against which a cover's payouts are judged; no real indemnity losses are
used.

### UK recalibration

Mishra et al. (2026) recalibrate the Schwierz model against PERILS industry
loss data (1999–2024) for 12 European countries using CLIMADA, with the same
hazard (C3S EWS footprints) and exposure (LitPop) as njord. The paper is a
preprint under review. One parameter is
fitted per country: the MDD curve is multiplied by a common factor and the
PAA is left unchanged. The fit is made separately with RMSE and RMSLE cost
functions. RMSE is driven by the largest events and fits the tail; RMSLE fits
the frequent, mid-range events. For the UK both lower the curve: the maximum
MDD is about 0.030 (RMSE) and 0.033 (RMSLE), against 0.0373 for the original,
factors of about 0.8 and 0.88. The paper gives these only in a figure
(Fig. 3m–n), so the factors are read by eye from it. njord uses
`mdd_scale = 0.8`, the RMSE fit, since the trigger is concerned with the
tail.

## Trigger

The trigger index in njord is an **exposure-weighted mean peak gust**,
computed for each storm event over a region as:

$$I = \frac{\sum_{i} w_i \cdot v_i}{\sum_i w_i}$$

where $v_i$ is the footprint gust (the storm's maximum 10-metre gust over
the 72-hour window) at grid cell $i$ and $w_i$ is the value of the LitPop
assets in that cell within the region (`exposure_weights()`,
`weighted_mean_index()`). The sum is over the cells with assets in the
region; a cell on a regional border counts in each region by its share of
the cell's UK land. Weighting by assets makes the index follow the gusts
where the insured value is.

Two designs are calibrated: one cover for the whole UK and a pair of covers,
one for England and Wales and one for Scotland, each on its own regional
index and losses, whose payouts are added.

The parametric payout follows a **linear ramp** structure:

$$P(I) = \begin{cases}
0 & I < A \\
L \cdot \dfrac{I - A}{E - A} & A \le I \le E \\
L & I > E
\end{cases}$$

where $A$ is the attachment (trigger) level, $E$ is the exhaustion level and
$L$ is the policy limit. Each cover is designed to pay a **layer** of its
region's losses: the loss above the 1-in-5 year loss (the retention), up to
the 1-in-20 year loss, so the limit $L$ is the difference between the two.
The return periods are illustrative and would be negotiated in a
real transaction. Three rules set $A$ and $E$:

- **R1**, `min_index_calibration()`: each level is the lowest index among
  the storms whose loss exceeds the retention or the 1-in-20 year loss.
- **R2**, `frequency_matching_calibration()`: as many storms trigger a
  payout as have a recovery, and as many receive the full limit as have a
  loss above the 1-in-20 year loss.
- **R3**, `fitted_ramp_calibration()`: the levels that minimise the sum
  over all storms of the squared basis risk, or of its absolute value.

## Basis risk

For each storm event $e$, the basis risk of a cover is defined as:

$$B_e = P_e - R_e$$

where $P_e$ is the parametric payout and $R_e$ is what the layer would
recover: the storm's modelled loss above the retention, capped at the limit
(`basis_risk()`), both expressed as fractions of the total UK assets.
Positive values indicate over-payment (the trigger pays more than the layer
would); negative values indicate under-payment (the insured bears a loss the
layer would have covered).

The distribution of $B_e$ across the historical event set characterises the
basis risk of the trigger design. It has two sources: storms whose index
passes the attachment but whose loss stays below the retention, which are
paid when the layer would pay nothing, and storms whose loss reaches the
layer but whose index stays low, which are paid too little or nothing.

Over the event set (1,323 storms, 1940–2025, the same for every cover) the
UK cover under R1 pays the largest storms in full, but 120 storms pay out
against 18 that would recover, so it pays about four times what the layer
would each year. Splitting the UK into an England and Wales cover and a
Scotland cover roughly halves the number of storms paid with nothing to
recover (49 against 103). It also pays in full
the storm that hit Scotland hardest (January 2002), which the UK cover
misses. The Scotland cover tracks its layer closely; the England and Wales
cover does not. The two regional covers together
are, however, a bigger cover than the UK one: their limits add up to USD
0.314 bn against 0.243 bn, and their layers would recover USD 0.036 bn a
year against 0.028 bn. So each cover is best judged against its own layer
rather than against the other. The figures come from the tables below.

## Results in sample

Basis risk here is measured against a modelled loss built from the same
ERA5 gust field as the index, so errors in that field are not part of it
(see [Limits](#limits)).

The event set is the package's current definition: the storms of
1940–2025 with a UK maximum gust above 25 m/s, less those that share a
maximum gust with a nearby storm (`shared_max_within_72h()`). A storm with
no gust values in a region (NA in the CSV) has index 0 there. Losses are
under the Schwierz curve with the MDD scaled by `mdd_scale`, as a fraction
of the total UK assets, so the covers' amounts can be added.

```{r settings}
first_year <- 1940
last_year <- 2025
gust_threshold <- 25
mdd_scale <- 0.8
attach_rp <- 5
exhaust_rp <- 20
block <- 5
n_boot <- 5000
seed <- 1
jennifer <- 1346
plot_min_index <- 25
```

```{r files}
file_names <- c(values = "uk_storm_values.csv",
                uk_index = "uk_exposure_gust.csv",
                uk_loss = "uk_storm_losses.csv",
                ew_index = "ew_exposure_gust.csv",
                ew_loss = "ew_storm_losses.csv",
                sco_index = "sco_exposure_gust.csv",
                sco_loss = "sco_storm_losses.csv",
                cover = "uk_nuts1_cover.tif",
                assets = "uk_litpop_025deg.tif",
                r3_insample = "insample_fitted_ramp.csv",
                r3_holdout = "holdout_fitted_ramp.csv")
files <- vapply(file_names, function(f)
  system.file("extdata", f, package = "njord"), character(1))
```

```{r events}
# One column of a per-storm CSV, keyed by track id, under a new name.
read_column <- function(file, name)
  setNames(read.csv(file), c("track_id", name))

storms <- read.csv(files[["values"]])
storms$central_time <- as.POSIXct(storms$central_time, tz = "UTC")
for (k in c("uk_index", "uk_loss", "ew_index", "ew_loss", "sco_index",
            "sco_loss"))
  storms <- merge(storms, read_column(files[[k]], k))

year <- lubridate::year(storms$central_time)
events <- subset(storms, !shared_max_within_72h(storms) &
                   max_gust > gust_threshold &
                   year >= first_year & year <= last_year)
scheme <- season_folds(first_year, last_year, block = block)
years <- sum(scheme$years)
events_per_year <- nrow(events) / years
total_assets <- sum(exposure_weights(files[["cover"]], files[["assets"]],
                                     regions = "UK")$weight)
usd_bn <- function(x) x * total_assets / 1e9
usd_m <- function(x) x * total_assets / 1e6

region_events <- function(region) {
  index <- events[[paste0(region, "_index")]]
  data.frame(event = events$track_id, central_time = events$central_time,
             index = ifelse(is.na(index), 0, index),
             loss = mdd_scale * events[[paste0(region, "_loss")]] /
               total_assets)
}
ev <- lapply(c(uk = "uk", ew = "ew", sco = "sco"), region_events)
c(storms = nrow(events), per_year = round(events_per_year, 2))
```

R1 and R2 are computed here. R3 takes minutes to fit, so its in-sample
levels are read from `inst/extdata/insample_fitted_ramp.csv`, written by
`inst/scripts/holdout_fitted_ramp.R`. The file's header records the
settings and storms it was made with; they are checked against those here
(code not shown), and the vignette stops if they differ.

```{r r3-check, echo = FALSE}
# The "# key: value" lines at the top of a precomputed file.
read_header <- function(file) {
  lines <- grep("^# [a-z_]+: ", readLines(file), value = TRUE)
  setNames(sub("^# [a-z_]+: ", "", lines),
           sub("^# ([a-z_]+): .*", "\\1", lines))
}

# Why a precomputed file's header and storms differ from what is expected
# here; empty if they don't.
stale_reasons <- function(header, expected, same_storms) {
  found <- header[names(expected)]
  bad <- is.na(found) | found != expected
  c(if (any(bad)) paste0(names(expected)[bad], " is ", found[bad],
                         " in the file but ", expected[bad], " here"),
    if (!same_storms) "its storms are not the event set here")
}

r3_insample <- read.csv(files[["r3_insample"]], comment.char = "#",
                        colClasses = c(attachment_events = "character",
                                       exhaustion_events = "character"))
expected <- vapply(list(first_year = first_year, last_year = last_year,
                        block = block, folds = max(scheme$fold),
                        events = nrow(events),
                        gust_threshold = gust_threshold,
                        mdd_scale = mdd_scale, attach_rp = attach_rp,
                        exhaust_rp = exhaust_rp), as.character, "")
insample_header <- read_header(files[["r3_insample"]])
stale <- stale_reasons(
  insample_header,
  c(expected, loss = "squared absolute", regions = "uk ew sco"),
  setequal(strsplit(insample_header["event_ids"], " ")[[1]],
           as.character(events$track_id)))
if (length(stale) > 0)
  stop("insample_fitted_ramp.csv does not match this vignette: ",
       paste(stale, collapse = "; "),
       ". Delete it and run inst/scripts/holdout_fitted_ramp.R.")
```

Each cover is a layer on its own region's losses. For each cover and rule
the attachment and exhaustion are set, each storm's payout and recovery
computed and the payouts scored against the recoveries. The combined cover
adds the England and Wales and Scotland payouts and recoveries storm by
storm; it has no levels of its own.

```{r in-sample}
# The loss with return period rp years, as in the calibration functions.
loss_at <- function(loss, rp, events_per_year)
  unname(quantile(loss, 1 - 1 / (rp * events_per_year)))

# Scores of a cover's payouts p against its recoveries r, storm by storm,
# as in holdout_summary(): the no-index cover pays every storm the mean
# recovery.
score <- function(p, r, years)
  c(paid = sum(p > 0), recovering = sum(r > 0),
    false_payments = sum(p > 0 & r == 0), misses = sum(r > 0 & p == 0),
    rms_basis_risk = sqrt(mean((p - r)^2)),
    rms_to_baseline = sqrt(sum((p - r)^2) / sum((mean(r) - r)^2)),
    paid_to_recovery = sum(p) / sum(r), correlation = cor(p, r),
    annual_payout = sum(p) / years, annual_recovery = sum(r) / years)

# The index of the first storm in a space-separated list of track ids.
setter_index <- function(region, setters)
  ev[[region]]$index[ev[[region]]$event == strsplit(setters, " ")[[1]][1]]

live <- list(R1 = min_index_calibration, R2 = frequency_matching_calibration)
r3_losses <- c(R3 = "squared", R3abs = "absolute")
in_sample <- lapply(setNames(names(ev), names(ev)), function(region) {
  e <- ev[[region]]
  index_vec <- setNames(e$index, e$event)
  loss_vec <- setNames(e$loss, e$event)
  retention <- loss_at(e$loss, attach_rp, events_per_year)
  limit <- loss_at(e$loss, exhaust_rp, events_per_year) - retention
  levels <- lapply(live, function(method)
    method(index_vec, loss_vec, attach_rp = attach_rp,
           exhaust_rp = exhaust_rp, events_per_year = events_per_year))
  # The stored levels are rounded, so each is replaced by the exact index
  # of the first storm recorded as setting it.
  for (k in names(r3_losses)) {
    row <- r3_insample[r3_insample$region == region &
                         r3_insample$loss == r3_losses[[k]], ]
    levels[[k]] <- list(
      attachment = setter_index(region, row$attachment_events),
      exhaustion = setter_index(region, row$exhaustion_events))
  }
  setter <- function(level) paste(e$event[e$index == level], collapse = " ")
  recovery <- pmin(pmax(e$loss - retention, 0), limit)
  list(retention = retention, limit = limit, recovery = recovery,
       rules = lapply(levels, function(lv)
         list(attachment = lv$attachment, exhaustion = lv$exhaustion,
              set_by = paste(setter(lv$attachment), "/",
                             setter(lv$exhaustion)),
              payout = payout(e$index, lv$attachment, lv$exhaustion,
                              limit))))
})
rules <- names(in_sample$sco$rules)
in_sample$combined <- list(
  retention = in_sample$ew$retention + in_sample$sco$retention,
  limit = in_sample$ew$limit + in_sample$sco$limit,
  recovery = in_sample$ew$recovery + in_sample$sco$recovery,
  rules = lapply(setNames(rules, rules), function(k)
    list(attachment = NA, exhaustion = NA, set_by = "",
         payout = in_sample$ew$rules[[k]]$payout +
           in_sample$sco$rules[[k]]$payout)))
in_sample_scores <- lapply(in_sample, function(cv)
  lapply(cv$rules, function(rl) score(rl$payout, cv$recovery, years)))
```

In each table, *paid* is the storms paid against the storms with a
recovery (above the retention), *false* the storms paid with no recovery
and *missed* the storms with a recovery but paid nothing. *RMS / no index*
is the RMS basis risk over that of a cover paying every storm the mean
recovery. Amounts are in USD.

```{r in-sample-table, echo = FALSE}
fmt <- function(x, digits = 2) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = digits)
rule_labels <- c(R1 = "R1 minimum index", R2 = "R2 frequency matching",
                 R3 = "R3 fitted ramp, squared",
                 R3abs = "R3 fitted ramp, absolute")
labels <- c(sco = "Scotland", ew = "England and Wales",
            combined = "England and Wales plus Scotland", uk = "UK")
layer_caption <- function(cv) {
  x <- in_sample[[cv]]
  paste0(labels[[cv]], if (cv == "combined") ", layers " else ", layer ",
         "USD ", fmt(usd_bn(x$limit), 3), " bn xs USD ",
         fmt(usd_bn(x$retention), 3), " bn",
         if (cv == "combined") " in all" else "",
         if (cv == "uk") " (the national-trigger contrast)" else "")
}
in_sample_table <- function(cv) {
  x <- in_sample[[cv]]
  knitr::kable(do.call(rbind, lapply(rules, function(k) {
    rl <- x$rules[[k]]
    s <- in_sample_scores[[cv]][[k]]
    data.frame(rule = rule_labels[[k]],
               `attach m/s` = if (cv == "combined") "-"
                 else fmt(rl$attachment),
               `exhaust m/s` = if (cv == "combined") "-"
                 else fmt(rl$exhaustion),
               `set by` = rl$set_by,
               paid = paste(s[["paid"]], "/", s[["recovering"]]),
               false = s[["false_payments"]], missed = s[["misses"]],
               `RMS USD m` = fmt(usd_m(s[["rms_basis_risk"]]), 1),
               `RMS / no index` = fmt(s[["rms_to_baseline"]]),
               `paid / layer` = fmt(s[["paid_to_recovery"]]),
               correlation = fmt(s[["correlation"]]),
               `USD m a year paid / recovered` =
                 paste(fmt(usd_m(s[["annual_payout"]]), 1), "/",
                       fmt(usd_m(s[["annual_recovery"]]), 1)),
               check.names = FALSE)
  })), align = "llllrrrrrrrl")
}
```

The ten storms with the largest UK loss under R1: their indices, the UK
cover's payout and recovery, the same for the two regional covers added and
the storm's loss, in USD bn.

```{r top-ten, echo = FALSE}
top <- order(-events$uk_loss)[1:10]
r1 <- function(cv) in_sample[[cv]]$rules$R1$payout
knitr::kable(data.frame(event = events$track_id[top],
                        uk_index = round(ev$uk$index[top], 1),
                        ew_index = round(ev$ew$index[top], 1),
                        sco_index = round(ev$sco$index[top], 1),
                        uk_payout = fmt(usd_bn(r1("uk")[top]), 3),
                        uk_layer = fmt(usd_bn(in_sample$uk$recovery[top]), 3),
                        regional_payout = fmt(usd_bn(r1("combined")[top]), 3),
                        regional_layer =
                          fmt(usd_bn(in_sample$combined$recovery[top]), 3),
                        storm_loss = fmt(usd_bn(ev$uk$loss[top]), 3)),
             align = "rrrrrrrrr")
```

For each R1 cover with an index, the payout ramp (line) and each storm's
recovery (points) against the cover's index, for storms with an index of
at least `plot_min_index`. A storm on the line is paid exactly what the
layer would pay; the vertical gap is its basis risk.

```{r r1-figure, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 6, dpi = 96, fig.retina = 2, out.width = "70%"}
plot_covers <- c(uk = "UK", ew = "England and Wales", sco = "Scotland")
by_cover <- function(f)
  do.call(rbind, lapply(names(plot_covers), function(k)
    data.frame(cover = factor(plot_covers[[k]], plot_covers),
               f(in_sample[[k]], ev[[k]]))))
storm_points <- by_cover(function(cv, e)
  data.frame(index = e$index, layer_loss = usd_bn(cv$recovery)))
ramps <- by_cover(function(cv, e) {
  rl <- cv$rules$R1
  x <- c(plot_min_index, rl$attachment, rl$exhaustion, max(e$index))
  data.frame(index = x, payout = usd_bn(payout(x, rl$attachment,
                                               rl$exhaustion, cv$limit)))
})
ggplot2::ggplot() +
  ggplot2::geom_point(
    data = subset(storm_points, index >= plot_min_index),
    ggplot2::aes(index, layer_loss), alpha = 0.4, size = 1) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(data = ramps, ggplot2::aes(index, payout),
                     colour = "firebrick") +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(~cover, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "Exposure-weighted mean gust index (m/s)",
                y = "USD bn",
                title = paste("R1 trigger payout (line) and layer",
                              "recovery (points), storm by storm")) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal()
```

## Out-of-sample test

The in-sample figures score each rule on the storms it was calibrated on;
here each storm is scored with a cover calibrated without it. The 87 storm
seasons (July to June) are split into 17 folds of 5 consecutive seasons,
the last taking the two left over, and each fold's storms are scored with
the layer and levels calibrated on the other 16 folds. The intervals are
90% intervals from `n_boot` resamples of the seasons, so they reflect only
which storms are scored. A fold whose rule cannot be fitted counts as no
cover (payout 0). R1 and R2 are computed here; R3 is read from
`inst/extdata/holdout_fitted_ramp.csv`, precomputed by
`inst/scripts/holdout_fitted_ramp.R`, and the vignette stops if its header
or storms do not match the settings and event set here (check not shown).

```{r r3-holdout-check, echo = FALSE}
r3_holdout <- read.csv(files[["r3_holdout"]], comment.char = "#",
                       colClasses = c(failure = "character"))
stale <- stale_reasons(
  read_header(files[["r3_holdout"]]),
  c(expected, loss = "squared", regions = "ew sco"),
  all(vapply(c("ew", "sco"), function(r)
    setequal(r3_holdout$event[r3_holdout$region == r], events$track_id),
    logical(1))))
if (length(stale) > 0)
  stop("holdout_fitted_ramp.csv does not match this vignette: ",
       paste(stale, collapse = "; "),
       ". Delete it and run inst/scripts/holdout_fitted_ramp.R.")
```

```{r holdout}
regional <- do.call(rbind, c(
  lapply(names(live), function(k)
    do.call(rbind, lapply(c("ew", "sco"), function(region)
      transform(holdout_calibration(ev[[region]], region, live[[k]],
                                    scheme = scheme, attach_rp = attach_rp,
                                    exhaust_rp = exhaust_rp),
                rule = k)))),
  list(transform(r3_holdout, rule = "R3"))))
combined <- combine_holdout(regional)
pooled <- rbind(regional[names(combined)], combined)
holdout <- holdout_summary(pooled, scheme, n_boot = n_boot, seed = seed)
failures <- holdout_failures(regional, scheme)
```

```{r holdout-table, echo = FALSE}
stat_of <- function(cv, k, statistic)
  unlist(holdout[holdout$region == cv & holdout$rule == k &
                   holdout$statistic == statistic,
                 c("estimate", "lower", "upper")])
with_interval <- function(x)
  paste0(fmt(x[1]), " [", fmt(x[2]), ", ", fmt(x[3]), "]")
knitr::kable(do.call(rbind, lapply(c("sco", "ew", "combined"), function(cv)
  do.call(rbind, lapply(c("R1", "R2", "R3"), function(k)
    data.frame(cover = labels[[cv]], rule = rule_labels[[k]],
               paid = paste(stat_of(cv, k, "paid")[1], "/",
                            stat_of(cv, k, "recovering")[1]),
               `paid / recovered` =
                 with_interval(stat_of(cv, k, "paid_to_recovery")),
               `RMS / flat payout` =
                 with_interval(stat_of(cv, k, "rms_to_baseline")),
               `failed folds` = stat_of(cv, k, "failed_folds")[1],
               check.names = FALSE))))),
  align = "lllllr", row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r holdout-failures, echo = FALSE}
season_label <- function(s) paste0(s, "/", substr(s + 1, 3, 4))
r1_ew <- failures[failures$rule == "R1" & failures$region == "ew", ]
```

R1 cannot be fitted for England and Wales in `r nrow(r1_ew)` folds
(`r paste(season_label(r1_ew$first_season), "to", season_label(r1_ew$last_season), collapse = ", ")`),
where one storm sets both levels; its RMS against a flat payout is
`r fmt(stat_of("ew", "R1", "rms_to_baseline")[1])` with those folds
counted as no cover and
`r fmt(stat_of("ew", "R1", "rms_to_baseline_fitted")[1])` with them left
out.

## Limits

These points come from checks run while the package was developed.

- **One gust field.** The index and the modelled loss are built from the
  same ERA5 gust footprints, so the basis risk measured here leaves out any
  error in that field. It is the basis risk against a model of the loss,
  not against real losses.
- **ERA5 against station gusts.** At named stations ERA5 minus the observed
  gust averages −7.7 m/s for the storm of October 1987 (6 stations) and
  for that of October 2013 (5 stations), −3.6 m/s for Ciara (7 stations,
  though +0.9 and +2.6 m/s at the two named Midlands and Yorkshire
  stations) and +2.4 m/s for January 2002 (12 stations, +7.5 to +9.6 m/s
  at Edinburgh and Glasgow airports). The station coordinates, and so the
  ERA5 cell matched to each station, are unverified, as is one October
  1987 observation (Manston).
- **January 2002 in Scotland.** The modelled Scottish loss for January
  2002 (track 1346) is not supported by those gusts. Scoring the hold-out
  without it changes the Scotland ratios by at most 0.02.
- **Damage curve.** The damage ratio rises
  `r round(schwierz_mdr(32, mdd_scale) / schwierz_mdr(27, mdd_scale), 1)`
  times from 27 to 32 m/s but
  `r round(schwierz_mdr(37, mdd_scale) / schwierz_mdr(32, mdd_scale), 1)`
  times from 32 to 37 m/s, so a small error in the gust makes a large
  error in the loss.
- **Missing storms.** The Hodges product, which the package uses, matches
  52 of the 77 storms named by the Met Office from 2015/16 to 2024/25, so
  about a third have no track, among them Arwen, Ciaran, Malik
  and Eowyn; PERILS puts the UK loss for Eowyn at GBP 378m
  ([Artemis, 26 January 2026](https://www.artemis.bm/news/perils-finalises-industry-loss-estimate-for-windstorm-eowyn-at-e765m/)).
  The TempestExtremes product matches 24 of the 77.
- **Before 1979.** The modelled annual loss triples after 1979, probably
  partly because ERA5 has less data to draw on before the satellite era.
- **Ciara and Dennis.** The modelled UK loss for Ciara and Dennis
  (February 2020) is about 2.75 times the ABI's early wind figure of
  GBP 149m. The conversion from USD at 1.30 per GBP is approximate and
  unverified.

## Planned refinements

The reference triggers are deliberately simple.
A number of refinements could be considered.

### 1. Zonal trigger (NUTS1 regions)

The two regional covers, England and Wales and Scotland, are a first step
towards a zonal trigger. They already reduce geographic basis risk, the
risk that a storm devastates one region while the UK-wide index stays below
the attachment: the Scotland cover pays the January 2002 storm that the UK
cover misses. The next step is a separate cover for each of the 12 UK NUTS1
regions (e.g. North West England, Wales, South East England), each with its
own index and layer, at the cost of additional complexity in the contract
specification. England and Wales in particular is large and varied, and its
cover tracks its losses much less closely than the Scotland cover does.

### 2. Multi-zone aggregate trigger

Extend the zonal approach to an aggregate structure: the payout is triggered
by a weighted sum of regional indices, with weights reflecting the insured
exposure distribution. This is analogous to the zonal SSI structures used in
some European cat bond transactions.

### 3. Trigger shape optimisation

The linear ramp is a natural starting point but not necessarily optimal. A
step trigger (binary payout at attachment) has maximum simplicity; a
polynomial ramp can be calibrated to match the indemnity loss curve more
closely in the tail. The optimal shape can be found by minimising the basis
risk variance subject to an actuarial fairness constraint using the
historical event set as training data.

### 4. Basis risk decomposition

The total basis risk variance can be decomposed into:

- **Geographic basis risk** — mismatch between the location of losses and the
  spatial footprint measured by the trigger index.
- **Temporal basis risk** — mismatch arising from the 72-hour integration
  window versus the actual loss accumulation period.
- **Structural basis risk** — residual mismatch after controlling for
  geography and timing, attributable to differences in vulnerability (e.g.
  industrial vs residential exposure) not captured by the damage model.

Basis risk of these kinds is described qualitatively by PwC (2024); the
decomposition of its variance into these three parts is the author's own
formulation.

### 5. Vulnerability sensitivity

Compare the basis risk under `mdd_scale` 1 (original), 0.8 (RMSE) and 0.88
(RMSLE). A single MDD factor scales every storm's loss alike, so the
attachment and exhaustion from `min_index_calibration()` do not change; only the
size of losses against payouts does. If the layer is defined by
return-period losses from the same scaled curve, payouts and recoveries
scale together and the comparison does not change, so the test is
informative only if the layer is fixed in dollars or the curve's shape
changes.

### 6. Convex indices

A mean gust index is linear in the gust, while wind damage is steeply
convex: under the Schwierz curve the loss at a cell grows much faster than
the gust. A storm with very high gusts over part of a region can cause a
large loss with only a moderate mean, and the effect is greatest in a large,
varied region such as England and Wales. Indices that give the highest
gusts more weight could follow losses more closely. Candidates are:

- **Gust cubed** — the exposure-weighted mean of $v_i^3$, with the cube
  root taken so that the index stays in m s⁻¹.
- **Excess gust** — following Klawa and Ulbrich (2003), the cubed excess of
  the gust over the local 98th percentile, $(v_i / V98_i - 1)^3$, summed
  over the cells where $v_i > V98_i$ and weighted by population or
  exposure. Measuring the gust against the local climate allows for
  buildings being built for the winds usual where they stand.
- **Storm Severity Index** (Leckebusch et al., 2008):

$$\text{SSI} = \sum_i \left(\frac{v_i}{V98_i} - 1\right)^3 w_i$$

where the sum is over grid cells where $v_i > V98_i$, $V98_i$ is the
98th percentile of the local gust distribution over a reference
climatological period (1991–2020) and $w_i$ is a cell weight.

The last two need a V98 surface. It has been computed from ERA5 daily
maximum gusts for 1991–2020 but is not yet part of the package.

### 7. Frequency–severity model and EP curves

A complete probabilistic view of the trigger requires modelling storm frequency
and severity separately. Storm frequency (annual event count above a minimum
gust threshold) would be fitted with a negative binomial distribution to
accommodate over-dispersion relative to a Poisson process. Storm severity
(modelled loss conditional on occurrence) would be fitted with a Generalised
Pareto Distribution to the exceedances above a threshold chosen by mean excess
plot inspection. Together these permit Monte Carlo simulation of an extended
event set from which occurrence and aggregate exceedance probability curves can
be derived for both indemnity losses and parametric payouts.
